claim: Drosophila melanogaster exhibits consolidated sleep during both day and night.
source: The fruit fly, Drosophila melanogaster, exhibits consolidated sleep during both day and night, with night sleep associated with higher arousal thresholds compared to day sleep.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a known characteristic of Drosophila sleep.

claim: Night sleep in Drosophila is associated with higher arousal thresholds compared to day sleep.
source: The fruit fly, Drosophila melanogaster, exhibits consolidated sleep during both day and night, with night sleep associated with higher arousal thresholds compared to day sleep.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: Neurocalcin (NCA) promotes sleep during the night but not the day.
source: Here we identify a role for the neuronal calcium sensor protein Neurocalcin (NCA) in promoting sleep during the night but not the day by suppressing nocturnal arousal and hyperactivity.
evidence: This is the main finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: NCA suppresses nocturnal arousal and hyperactivity.
source: Here we identify a role for the neuronal calcium sensor protein Neurocalcin (NCA) in promoting sleep during the night but not the day by suppressing nocturnal arousal and hyperactivity.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by arousal threshold experiments and locomotor activity data.

claim: Both circadian and light-sensing pathways define the temporal window in which NCA promotes sleep.
source: We show that both circadian and light-sensing pathways define the temporal window in which NCA promotes sleep.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experiments in different light/dark conditions.

claim: NCA promotes sleep by suppressing synaptic release from a dispersed wake-promoting neural network.
source: Furthermore, we find that NCA promotes sleep by suppressing synaptic release from a dispersed wake-promoting neural network and demonstrate that the mushroom bodies, a sleep-regulatory center, are a module within this network.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by synaptopHluorin imaging experiments.

claim: The mushroom bodies are a module within the wake-promoting neural network regulated by NCA.
source: Furthermore, we find that NCA promotes sleep by suppressing synaptic release from a dispersed wake-promoting neural network and demonstrate that the mushroom bodies, a sleep-regulatory center, are a module within this network.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by genetic manipulation and imaging experiments.

claim: Sleep influences neuronal development.
source: Sleep is a widely conserved behavior that influences numerous aspects of brain function, including neuronal development (Kayser et al., 2014), clearance of metabolic waste (Xie et al., 2013), synaptic plasticity (Havekes et al., 2016; Kuhn et al., 2016; Li et al., 2017; Yang et al., 2014), and complex behaviors (Kayser et al., 2015; Kayser et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation support.

claim: Sleep influences clearance of metabolic waste.
source: Sleep is a widely conserved behavior that influences numerous aspects of brain function, including neuronal development (Kayser et al., 2014), clearance of metabolic waste (Xie et al., 2013), synaptic plasticity (Havekes et al., 2016; Kuhn et al., 2016; Li et al., 2017; Yang et al., 2014), and complex behaviors (Kayser et al., 2015; Kayser et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation support.

claim: Sleep influences synaptic plasticity.
source: Sleep is a widely conserved behavior that influences numerous aspects of brain function, including neuronal development (Kayser et al., 2014), clearance of metabolic waste (Xie et al., 2013), synaptic plasticity (Havekes et al., 2016; Kuhn et al., 2016; Li et al., 2017; Yang et al., 2014), and complex behaviors (Kayser et al., 2015; Kayser et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation support.

claim: Drosophila sleep is characterized by immobility, altered posture and elevated arousal threshold during both day and night.
source: The fruit fly, Drosophila, exhibits a sleep-like state characterized by immobility, altered posture and elevated arousal threshold during both day and night (Hendricks et al., 2000; Shaw et al., 2000).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation support.

claim: Sleep in Drosophila is regulated by circadian and homeostatic processes.
source: Similarly to mammals, sleep in Drosophila is regulated by circadian and homeostatic processes (Huber et al., 2004; Liu et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation support.

claim: Human sleep can be separated into stages of differing arousal thresholds (REM and three non-REM sleep stages).
source: Furthermore, just as human sleep can be separated into stages of differing arousal thresholds (REM and three non-REM sleep stages) (Rechtschaffen et al., 1966), sleep in Drosophila also varies in intensity throughout the day/night cycle, with night sleep having a higher arousal threshold relative to day sleep (Faville et al., 2015; van Alphen et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation support.

claim: Sleep in Drosophila varies in intensity throughout the day/night cycle.
source: Furthermore, just as human sleep can be separated into stages of differing arousal thresholds (REM and three non-REM sleep stages) (Rechtschaffen et al., 1966), sleep in Drosophila also varies in intensity throughout the day/night cycle, with night sleep having a higher arousal threshold relative to day sleep (Faville et al., 2015; van Alphen et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation support.

claim: Mutations in a select number of genes modulate either day or night sleep in Drosophila.
source: In Drosophila, mutations in a select number of genes modulate either day or night sleep, suggesting that distinct genetic pathways may promote or inhibit these sleep stages (Ishimoto et al., 2012; Tomita et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation support.

claim: Distinct genetic pathways may promote or inhibit different sleep stages in Drosophila.
source: In Drosophila, mutations in a select number of genes modulate either day or night sleep, suggesting that distinct genetic pathways may promote or inhibit these sleep stages (Ishimoto et al., 2012; Tomita et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as a suggestion based on cited evidence.

claim: Drosophila NCA is highly homologous to the mammalian neuronal calcium sensor Hippocalcin, sharing >90% amino-acid identity.
source: Drosophila NCA is highly homologous to the mammalian neuronal calcium sensor Hippocalcin, sharing >90% amino-acid identity (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by the amino acid alignment figure.

claim: Neuronal expression of three independent RNAi lines targeting Nca mRNA reduced night sleep but not day sleep in adult male flies housed under 12L:12D conditions at 25°C.
source: Using the pan-neuronal driver elav-Gal4, we found that neuronal expression of three independent RNAi lines targeting Nca mRNA (kk108825, hmj21533 and jf03398; termed kk, hmj and jf respectively) reduced night sleep but not day sleep in adult male flies housed under 12 hr light: 12 hr dark conditions (12L: 12D) at 25°C (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–E), as measured by the Drosophila Activity Monitoring (DAM) system (Pfeiffenberger et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by experimental data in the supplementary figures.

claim: Sleep loss in flies expressing Nca RNAi correlated with significant reductions in Nca expression.
source: Sleep loss in flies expressing Nca RNAi correlated with significant reductions in Nca expression (Figure 1—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by qPCR data.

claim: Expression of the cg7646 locus was unaffected by Nca knockdown.
source: In contrast, expression of the cg7646 locus, which shares 5' regulatory elements with Nca and encodes a neuronal calcium sensor more closely related to mammalian Recoverin than Hippocalcin, was unaffected by Nca knockdown (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,G).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by qPCR data.

claim: Night-specific sleep loss following Nca knockdown was observed in virgin adult female flies.
source: Night-specific sleep loss following Nca knockdown was also observed in virgin adult female flies and in male flies expressing the kk Nca RNAi using other pan-neuronal or broadly expressed drivers (Figure 1—figure supplement 2H–J), whereas knockdown of cg7646 by RNAi did not impact night sleep (Figure 1—figure supplement 2K).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by experimental data.

claim: Knockdown of cg7646 by RNAi did not impact night sleep.
source: Night-specific sleep loss following Nca knockdown was also observed in virgin adult female flies and in male flies expressing the kk Nca RNAi using other pan-neuronal or broadly expressed drivers (Figure 1—figure supplement 2H–J), whereas knockdown of cg7646 by RNAi did not impact night sleep (Figure 1—figure supplement 2K).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by experimental data.

claim: Night sleep in Nca knockdown males appeared further reduced under short photoperiod conditions (8L:16D).
source: Interestingly, we found that night sleep in Nca knockdown males appeared even further reduced under short photoperiod conditions (8L: 16D) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by the sleep profile data in Figure 1A.

claim: In 8L:16D conditions, day sleep was unaffected whilst night sleep was reduced in Nca knockdown flies.
source: Similarly to 12L: 12D, in 8L: 16D day sleep was unaffected whilst night sleep was reduced (Figure 1A–C), due to fragmentation of consolidated sleep bouts during the middle of the night (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data in Figure 1.

claim: Night sleep reduction in Nca knockdown flies in 8L:16D was due to fragmentation of consolidated sleep bouts during the middle of the night.
source: Similarly to 12L: 12D, in 8L: 16D day sleep was unaffected whilst night sleep was reduced (Figure 1A–C), due to fragmentation of consolidated sleep bouts during the middle of the night (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by sleep bout analysis.

claim: Knockdown of Nca in neurons did not alter circadian rhythmicity.
source: Importantly, knockdown of Nca in neurons did not alter circadian rhythmicity (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by circadian rhythm analysis.

claim: Knockdown of Nca specifically in clock neurons did not affect night sleep.
source: Furthermore, knockdown of Nca specifically in clock neurons did not affect night sleep (see below).
evidence: This is stated in the results and refers to data presented later in the manuscript.

claim: Sleep loss in Nca knockdown flies is unlikely to be due to circadian clock dysfunction.
source: Thus, it is unlikely that sleep loss in Nca knockdown flies is due to circadian clock dysfunction.
evidence: This is an inference based on the circadian rhythm and clock neuron knockdown data.

claim: Three independent Nca null alleles were generated by replacing the entire Nca locus with a mini-white+ sequence using ends-out homologous recombination.
source: To provide further genetic evidence that NCA is a sleep-regulatory factor, we generated three independent Nca null alleles by replacing the entire Nca locus (including 5' and 3' UTRs) with a mini-white+ sequence using ends-out homologous recombination (Baena-Lopez et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the results and describes the method used to generate knockout alleles.

claim: No Nca mRNA expression was detected in homozygotes for the deleted Nca locus.
source: As expected, no Nca mRNA expression was detected in homozygotes for the deleted Nca locus (Figure 1—figure supplement 6D–E).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by RT-PCR and qPCR data.

claim: Male homozygotes and transheterozygotes for the three Nca knockout alleles exhibited normal day sleep but reduced night sleep.
source: Following outcrossing into an isogenic iso31 control background, male homozygotes and transheterozygotes for the three Nca knockout alleles were viable to the adult stage and exhibited normal day sleep but reduced night sleep, as measured by both DAM and DART systems (Figure 1G–L, Figure 1—figure supplement 7), similarly to Nca knockdown flies.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by sleep data from multiple measurement systems.

claim: NcaKO1 males displayed prolonged activity relative to controls following lights-off and frequent bouts of movement in the middle of the night.
source: By examining locomotor patterns in individual flies using the DART system, we found that NcaKO1 males consistently displayed prolonged activity relative to controls following lights-off and frequent bouts of movement even in the middle of the night – a period of quiescence in iso31 controls (Figure 1M,N).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by individual fly locomotor tracking data.

claim: Loss of NCA led to a reduction in average locomotor velocity across 24 hr.
source: Video-based analysis of waking locomotor velocities revealed that loss of NCA led to a reduction in average locomotor velocity across 24 hr (Figure 1—figure supplement 8A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by velocity analysis data.

claim: Loss of NCA reduced locomotor activity during the evening activity peak and following lights-off.
source: This was primarily driven by reduced locomotor activity during the evening activity peak and following lights-off, suggesting loss of NCA mildly reduces peak levels of activity (Figure 1—figure supplement 8C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by velocity analysis data.

claim: Locomotor velocities during normally quiescent periods of the night were greatly enhanced in NcaKO1 males compared to iso31 controls.
source: In contrast, locomotor velocities during normally quiescent periods of the night were greatly enhanced in NcaKO1 males compared to iso31 controls (Figure 1—figure supplement 8D), consistent with a perturbed sleep state.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by velocity analysis data.

claim: NCA promotes night sleep in Drosophila by acting in neurons.
source: Collectively, the above data demonstrate that NCA promotes night sleep in Drosophila and does so by acting in neurons.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the collective experimental data presented.

claim: Responsiveness during sleep stages in Drosophila is dynamically regulated, with night sleep exhibiting a higher arousal threshold relative to day sleep.
source: Recent studies have shown that responsiveness during sleep stages in Drosophila is dynamically regulated, with night sleep exhibiting a higher arousal threshold relative to day sleep (Faville et al., 2015; van Alphen et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the results with citation support.

claim: At ZT4, Nca knockdown did not significantly alter the arousal threshold.
source: At ZT4, we found that the majority of adult males from both control lines exhibited startle responses in response to vibration stimuli, and that Nca knockdown did not significantly alter the arousal threshold at this time point (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by arousal threshold data.

claim: The percentage of NcaKD flies responding to vibration stimulus was significantly higher at ZT16 relative to both control lines.
source: In contrast, the percentage of NcaKD flies responding to vibration stimulus was significantly higher at ZT16 relative to both control lines (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by arousal threshold data.

claim: There was no significant day/night difference in responsiveness to vibration stimulus in NcaKD flies.
source: Furthermore, whereas the percentage of control flies responding to vibration stimulus was significantly higher during the day compared to the night (elav > + and + > kk: p<0.0005, Binomial test with Bonferonni correction for multiple comparisons), there was no significant day/night difference in responsiveness in NcaKD flies (p=0.1).
evidence: This is stated in the results with statistical analysis.

claim: NCA is a molecular regulator of nighttime arousal in Drosophila.
source: These data suggest that NCA is a molecular regulator of nighttime arousal in Drosophila.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the arousal threshold experiments.

claim: In DD, robust sleep loss in NcaKD flies was restricted to the subjective night.
source: Initially, we examined sleep patterns in NcaKD flies under DD conditions, in which the circadian clock alone distinguishes subjective day from night. Interestingly, in DD robust sleep loss in NcaKD flies was still restricted to the subjective night (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by sleep data in constant dark conditions.

claim: The circadian clock intersects with NCA function.
source: These data suggest that the circadian clock intersects with NCA and demonstrate that sleep loss in NcaKD flies is not simply due to darkness-induced hyperactivity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the DD experiment results.

claim: Sleep loss in NcaKD flies is not simply due to darkness-induced hyperactivity.
source: These data suggest that the circadian clock intersects with NCA and demonstrate that sleep loss in NcaKD flies is not simply due to darkness-induced hyperactivity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the DD experiment results.

claim: In a timeless knockout background in DD, sleep loss in NcaKD flies was observed throughout the 24 hr dark period.
source: In a timeless knockout (timKO) background in DD (Lamaze et al., 2017), where the clock no longer demarcates subjective day from night, sleep loss in NcaKD flies was observed throughout the 24 hr dark period (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by sleep data in arrhythmic conditions.

claim: In a timKO background in 8L:16D conditions, significant sleep loss in NcaKD flies was observed during the night but not during the day.
source: Intriguingly, in a timKO background in 8L: 16D conditions, significant sleep loss in NcaKD flies was observed during the night (Figure 3E,F), but not during the day (elav > kk, timKO vs elav > +, timKO: p=0.75, Kruskal-Wallis test with Dunn's post-hoc test).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by sleep data.

claim: Light is capable of inhibiting sleep loss in NcaKD flies.
source: Thus, light is also capable of inhibiting sleep loss in NcaKD flies.
evidence: This is an inference based on the timKO experiment in 8L:16D conditions.

claim: Under constant light conditions, sleep loss in NcaKD flies was completely suppressed.
source: Consistent with this finding, under constant light (LL) conditions, in which the circadian clock becomes arrhythmic due to light-dependent degradation of Timeless (Hunter-Ensor et al., 1996; Koh et al., 2006; Peschel et al., 2006), sleep loss in NcaKD flies was completely suppressed (Figure 3G,H).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by sleep data in constant light.

claim: The circadian clock is not required for NCA to regulate sleep per se, but instead defines when NCA promotes sleep.
source: From the above data we draw two conclusions. Firstly, that the circadian clock is not required for NCA to regulate sleep per se, but instead defines when NCA promotes sleep.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experiments in different light/dark conditions.

claim: Light-sensing pathways suppress enhanced wakefulness resulting from reduced NCA expression.
source: Secondly, that light-sensing pathways suppress enhanced wakefulness resulting from reduced NCA expression.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experiments in different light/dark conditions.

claim: Ablation of photoreceptor cells through expression of gmr-hid did not alter sleep in NcaKD flies in LL.
source: Ablation of photoreceptor cells through expression of the pro-apoptotic gene hid (gmr-hid) did not alter sleep in NcaKD flies in LL (Figure 3I,J).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by sleep data.

claim: Loss of CRY in LL resulted in a small but significant loss of sleep in NcaKD flies.
source: In contrast, using a loss of function allele of cry (cry02), we found that loss of CRY in LL resulted in a small but significant loss of sleep in NcaKD flies (Figure 3K,L).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by sleep data.

claim: Additional light-sensing pathways act in concert with CRY to inhibit wakefulness in NcaKD flies in the presence of light.
source: However, the reduction in sleep in NcaKD, cry02 flies in LL is lower in magnitude compared to NcaKD flies in DD or 8L: 16D (Figures 1B and 3A), suggesting that additional light-sensing pathways act in concert with CRY to inhibit wakefulness in NcaKD flies in the presence of light.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparing sleep loss magnitudes across different conditions.

claim: Nca knockdown using two enhancer-Gal4 lines (R72C01 and R14A05) strongly reduced night sleep in 8L:16D conditions.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, we generated a series of driver line combinations and found that Nca knockdown using two enhancer-Gal4 lines (R72C01 – an enhancer in the Dop1R1 locus, and R14A05 – an enhancer in the single-minded locus; we refer to these drivers as C01 and A05 respectively) strongly reduced night sleep in 8L: 16D conditions (Figure 4A,B) (Jenett et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by sleep data.

claim: Nca knockdown using either C01 or A05 enhancer alone did not affect night sleep.
source: Nca knockdown using either enhancer alone did not affect night sleep (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–D), nor in combination with dopaminergic, Dop1R1-expressing or cry-expressing neurons, or components of the anterior visual pathway (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by sleep data.

claim: NCA expression in both C01- and A05-neurons is necessary for normal levels of night sleep.
source: The above data indicate that NCA expression in both C01- and A05-neurons is necessary for normal levels of night sleep.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the combinatorial knockdown experiments.

claim: Knockdown of Nca in C01- and A05-neurons resulted in sleep loss during the subjective night in DD.
source: Similarly to pan-neuronal NcaKD flies, knockdown of Nca in C01- and A05-neurons also resulted in sleep loss during the subjective night in DD (Figure 4C,D), no sleep loss in LL (Figure 4E,F), no alteration in daytime arousal threshold (Figure 4G), and a reduced arousal threshold during the night (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by sleep and arousal data.

claim: Knockdown of Nca in C01- and A05-neurons resulted in no sleep loss in LL.
source: Similarly to pan-neuronal NcaKD flies, knockdown of Nca in C01- and A05-neurons also resulted in sleep loss during the subjective night in DD (Figure 4C,D), no sleep loss in LL (Figure 4E,F), no alteration in daytime arousal threshold (Figure 4G), and a reduced arousal threshold during the night (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by sleep data.

claim: Knockdown of Nca in C01- and A05-neurons resulted in no alteration in daytime arousal threshold.
source: Similarly to pan-neuronal NcaKD flies, knockdown of Nca in C01- and A05-neurons also resulted in sleep loss during the subjective night in DD (Figure 4C,D), no sleep loss in LL (Figure 4E,F), no alteration in daytime arousal threshold (Figure 4G), and a reduced arousal threshold during the night (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by arousal data.

claim: Knockdown of Nca in C01- and A05-neurons resulted in a reduced arousal threshold during the night.
source: Similarly to pan-neuronal NcaKD flies, knockdown of Nca in C01- and A05-neurons also resulted in sleep loss during the subjective night in DD (Figure 4C,D), no sleep loss in LL (Figure 4E,F), no alteration in daytime arousal threshold (Figure 4G), and a reduced arousal threshold during the night (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by arousal data.

claim: The A05 enhancer drives expression in approximately 70 neurons.
source: The A05 enhancer drives expression in approximately 70 neurons (70.3 ± 4.7, n = 3), as quantified using a fluorescent nuclear marker (Barolo et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the results with quantification data.

claim: The C01 enhancer drives expression in approximately 240 neurons.
source: The C01 enhancer drives expression in approximately 240 neurons (239.7 ± 7.8, n = 3) which encompass MB-KCs as well as neurons projecting to the MB γ-lobes, the antennal mechanosensory and motor center (AMMC), and the superior medial protocerebrum (SMP) (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is stated in the results with quantification data.

claim: The C01 and A05 enhancers label non-overlapping regions of the MB, with C01 expressed in the αβ-KCs, and A05 expressed in α'β'-KCs.
source: Detailed examination within MB-KCs using standardized confocal images from the Virtual Fly Brain indicated that the C01 and A05 enhancers label non-overlapping regions of the MB, with C01 expressed in the αβ-KCs, and A05 expressed in α'β'-KCs (Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by imaging data.

claim: Nca knockdown in the MB-KCs using the ok107-Gal4 driver did not alter day or night sleep in 8L:16D.
source: Similarly to Nca knockdown in C01- and A05-neurons alone (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–D), Nca knockdown in the MB-KCs using the ok107-Gal4 driver did not alter day or night sleep in 8L: 16D (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B,C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by sleep data.

claim: Simultaneous knockdown of Nca in ok107- and A05-neurons significantly reduced night sleep.
source: However, simultaneous knockdown of Nca in ok107- and A05-neurons significantly reduced night sleep (Figure 5—figure supplement 2D,E), whereas Nca knockdown in both ok107- and C01-neurons did not (Figure 5—figure supplement 2F,G).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by sleep data.

claim: Nca knockdown in both ok107- and C01-neurons did not significantly reduce night sleep.
source: However, simultaneous knockdown of Nca in ok107- and A05-neurons significantly reduced night sleep (Figure 5—figure supplement 2D,E), whereas Nca knockdown in both ok107- and C01-neurons did not (Figure 5—figure supplement 2F,G).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by sleep data.

claim: The MB-KCs are a relevant component of the C01 expression domain.
source: Since Nca knockdown in ok107- and A05-neurons partially phenocopies the sleep-inhibiting effect of Nca knockdown in C01- and A05-neurons, these data suggest that the MB-KCs are a relevant component of the C01 expression domain.
evidence: This is an inference based on the combinatorial knockdown experiments.

claim: Nca knockdown in C01-neurons significantly increased the number of flies aroused by mechanical stimuli during the night but not the day.
source: Using the DART system, we found that Nca knockdown in either C01-neurons or in the MB-KCs (using ok107-Gal4) significantly increased the number of flies aroused by mechanical stimuli during the night but not the day (Figure 6A–D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by arousal threshold data.

claim: Nca knockdown in the MB-KCs significantly increased the number of flies aroused by mechanical stimuli during the night but not the day.
source: Using the DART system, we found that Nca knockdown in either C01-neurons or in the MB-KCs (using ok107-Gal4) significantly increased the number of flies aroused by mechanical stimuli during the night but not the day (Figure 6A–D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by arousal threshold data.

claim: NCA acts within the MB αβ-KCs to suppress nocturnal arousal.
source: Since the MB αβ-KCs are labelled by both the ok107-Gal4 and C01-Gal4 drivers, the above data collectively suggest that NCA acts within the MB αβ-KCs to suppress nocturnal arousal, and that additional circuits within the A05-positive domain are required in concert with C01-neurons (including MB αβ-KCs) to drive nocturnal hyperactivity when Nca expression is reduced.
evidence: This is an inference based on the arousal threshold experiments and driver expression patterns.

claim: Additional circuits within the A05-positive domain are required in concert with C01-neurons to drive nocturnal hyperactivity when Nca expression is reduced.
source: Since the MB αβ-KCs are labelled by both the ok107-Gal4 and C01-Gal4 drivers, the above data collectively suggest that NCA acts within the MB αβ-KCs to suppress nocturnal arousal, and that additional circuits within the A05-positive domain are required in concert with C01-neurons (including MB αβ-KCs) to drive nocturnal hyperactivity when Nca expression is reduced.
evidence: This is an inference based on the sleep and arousal experiments.

claim: At ZT9-11 in 8L:16D conditions, Nca knockdown in C01- and A05-neurons resulted in significantly enhanced synaptic release from the MB αβ-lobes and the AMMC.
source: At ZT9-11 in 8L: 16D conditions, Nca knockdown in C01- and A05-neurons resulted in significantly enhanced synaptic release from the MB αβ-lobes and the AMMC (Figure 7A,B) but not the MB γ-lobe region or the SMP (Figure 7C,D), demonstrating that NCA inhibits synaptic release from a subset of C01- and A05-neurons and supporting a physiological role for NCA in the MB αβ-lobes.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by synaptopHluorin imaging data.

claim: Nca knockdown in C01- and A05-neurons did not enhance synaptic release from the MB γ-lobe region or the SMP at ZT9-11 in 8L:16D.
source: At ZT9-11 in 8L: 16D conditions, Nca knockdown in C01- and A05-neurons resulted in significantly enhanced synaptic release from the MB αβ-lobes and the AMMC (Figure 7A,B) but not the MB γ-lobe region or the SMP (Figure 7C,D), demonstrating that NCA inhibits synaptic release from a subset of C01- and A05-neurons and supporting a physiological role for NCA in the MB αβ-lobes.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by synaptopHluorin imaging data.

claim: NCA inhibits synaptic release from a subset of C01- and A05-neurons.
source: At ZT9-11 in 8L: 16D conditions, Nca knockdown in C01- and A05-neurons resulted in significantly enhanced synaptic release from the MB αβ-lobes and the AMMC (Figure 7A,B) but not the MB γ-lobe region or the SMP (Figure 7C,D), demonstrating that NCA inhibits synaptic release from a subset of C01- and A05-neurons and supporting a physiological role for NCA in the MB αβ-lobes.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the synaptopHluorin imaging data.

claim: At CT9-11 in LL conditions, Nca knockdown in C01- and A05-neurons did not enhance synaptic release from the MB αβ-lobes, the MB γ-lobe region or the SMP.
source: Indeed, at Circadian Time (CT) 9–11 in LL conditions, Nca knockdown in C01- and A05-neurons did not enhance synaptic release from the MB αβ-lobes, the MB γ-lobe region or the SMP, and surprisingly, reduced synaptic release from the AMMC (Figure 7E–H).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by synaptopHluorin imaging data.

claim: At CT9-11 in LL conditions, Nca knockdown in C01- and A05-neurons reduced synaptic release from the AMMC.
source: Indeed, at Circadian Time (CT) 9–11 in LL conditions, Nca knockdown in C01- and A05-neurons did not enhance synaptic release from the MB αβ-lobes, the MB γ-lobe region or the SMP, and surprisingly, reduced synaptic release from the AMMC (Figure 7E–H).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by synaptopHluorin imaging data.

claim: Light-sensing pathways suppress both sleep loss and elevated synaptic release in the MB αβ-lobes and AMMC following Nca knockdown in C01- and A05-neurons.
source: Thus, light-sensing pathways suppress both sleep loss (Figure 4E,F) and elevated synaptic release in the MB αβ-lobes and AMMC following Nca knockdown in C01- and A05-neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on comparing imaging data in different light conditions.

claim: Excitation of A05-neurons did not alter night sleep at the activating temperature.
source: At the activating temperature, excitation of A05-neurons did not alter night sleep (Figure 8C,D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by TrpA1 activation experiments.

claim: Excitation of C01-neurons profoundly reduced night sleep as well as day sleep.
source: In contrast, excitation of C01-neurons profoundly reduced night sleep (Figure 8C,D) as well as day sleep (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by TrpA1 activation experiments.

claim: Simultaneous activation of C01- and A05-neurons further reduced night but not day sleep relative to activation of C01-neurons alone.
source: Interestingly, simultaneous activation of C01- and A05-neurons further reduced night but not day sleep relative to activation of C01-neurons alone, despite activation of A05-neurons alone having no impact on sleep in 8L: 16D (Figure 8C,D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by TrpA1 activation experiments.

claim: C01- and A05-neurons synergistically interact to modulate night sleep.
source: C01- and A05-neurons thus synergistically interact to modulate night sleep.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the TrpA1 activation experiments.

claim: Silencing C01- and A05-neurons with dORKΔC2 in an otherwise wild type background did not alter day or night sleep levels.
source: Silencing C01- and A05-neurons with dORKΔC2 in an otherwise wild type background did not alter day or night sleep levels (Figure 8E,F; p>0.99 compared to dORKΔC2/+controls, Kruskal-Wallis test with Dunn's post-hoc test).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by sleep data.

claim: Expression of dORKΔC2 in concert with Nca RNAi significantly suppressed night sleep loss relative to male flies expressing Nca RNAi alone.
source: However, consistent with the above prediction, expression of dORKΔC2 in concert with Nca RNAi significantly suppressed night sleep loss relative to male flies expressing Nca RNAi alone or alongside an innocuous transgene (UAS-FRT-stop-FRT-GFP) (p<0.0005).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by sleep data.

claim: NCA promotes night sleep by limiting synaptic output from arousal- and wake-promoting neurons within the C01- and A05-Gal4 domains that include the MB αβ-KCs.
source: Thus, NCA promotes night sleep by limiting synaptic output from arousal- and wake-promoting neurons within the C01- and A05-Gal4 domains that include the MB αβ-KCs.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the collective experimental data.

claim: NCA is not required within a single cell-type or neuropil region to inhibit nighttime arousal and wakefulness.
source: Our results are consistent with these findings and offer a tentative explanation for the difficulties in defining circuit requirements for sleep-relevant proteins in Drosophila. We show that NCA is not required within a single cell-type or neuropil region to inhibit nighttime arousal and wakefulness.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a conclusion from the results.

claim: Sleep-relevant NCA activity is necessary within two distinct domains of the Drosophila nervous system defined by the A05- and C01-Gal4 drivers.
source: Instead, sleep-relevant NCA activity is necessary within two distinct domains of the Drosophila nervous system defined by the A05- and C01-Gal4 drivers (Jenett et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a conclusion from the results.

claim: Reduced NCA activity in C01- and A05-neurons causes a mild elevation in neurotransmitter release from neuronal subsets within the C01- and A05-domains.
source: Since this thermo-genetic approach avoids unforeseen effects of chronic alterations in excitability on cellular processes (Depetris-Chauvin et al., 2011), the above data collectively support a model in which reduced NCA activity in C01- and A05-neurons causes a mild elevation in neurotransmitter release from neuronal subsets within the C01- and A05-domains.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a model based on the experimental data.

claim: Reduced NCA activity in C01- or A05-neurons alone is insufficient to promote wakefulness.
source: Reduced NCA activity in C01- or A05-neurons alone is insufficient to promote wakefulness.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as part of the proposed model.

claim: When NCA expression is inhibited in C01- and A05-neurons simultaneously, the resulting enhancement of synaptic output within this wider network is sufficient to reduce night sleep.
source: Yet when NCA expression is inhibited in C01- and A05-neurons simultaneously, the resulting enhancement of synaptic output within this wider network is sufficient to reduce night sleep.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as part of the proposed model.

claim: Thermo-genetic activation of MB αβ-lobes does not affect sleep levels.
source: Recent data has shown that thermo-genetic activation of MB αβ-lobes does not affect sleep levels (Sitaraman et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citation support.

claim: NCA plays dual functions in modulating arousal and wakefulness, likely by acting in distinct circuits within the fly brain.
source: Thus, NCA plays dual functions in modulating arousal and wakefulness, likely by acting in distinct circuits within the fly brain.

claim: Hippocalcin facilitates NMDA receptor endocytosis during LTD.
source: Hippocalcin facilitates NMDA receptor endocytosis during LTD and gates the slow afterhyperpolarisation, a calcium-activated potassium current controlling spike frequency adaptation (Andrade et al., 2012; Jo et al., 2010; Tzingounis et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citation support.

claim: NCA is broadly expressed in the Drosophila brain.
source: Indeed, cell-type-specific expression of homologous NCA-binding proteins may explain why synaptic output is enhanced in only a subset of C01- and A05-neurons following Nca knockdown, despite previous results showing that NCA is broadly expressed in the Drosophila brain (Teng et al., 1994).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citation support.
